text: Rocket launches often slip by a few days. Near the Moon's south pole, that can decide everything. Slipday asks: if the launch slips, can we still land here?
The answer is yes, not sure, or no. Here: yes, with eight days of slip margin, checked at thirteen touchdown points around the target.
This line is the challenge's goal: where the Sun and the Earth stand against the real horizon at touchdown, in numbers, with their paths drawn below.
Type how many days the launch slipped. Nine days: no. The Earth sinks behind distant ground, so radio contact falls short.
Missed the window? December still works. Other sites can work in January, though most are fragile. And one click downloads the whole answer.
Here is the real ground in 3-D, from NASA's laser measurements. The low Sun drags long shadows across it.
You can type your own spot right on the card. Here the answer is no: the Earth is hidden when it lands.
The map shows how many days of slip each spot survives. Red crosses mark where NASA's finer twenty-metre terrain disagrees.
Detail matters. At the Shackleton ridge, the eighty-metre map says yes. The twenty and five-metre maps say not sure.
Is the ground flat enough? Here, only just: the steepest spot sits right at NASA's goal for its crewed lander.
A lander does not come down exactly on target, so this gives the chance the ground under it is flat enough, for three kinds of lander.
A real test: the IM-1 lander. The app says yes for the February window it flew, and for the January one it missed.
NASA keeps nine Artemis regions, because one is not enough. The best one is open at twenty-eight point one percent of landing times.
The atlas runs that check for nine years. The weak season comes a little earlier every year.
When the Earth is hidden, a relay satellite circling the Moon could pass messages on. The main answer still counts the Earth alone.
You can also listen to the landing window: a high tone for the Sun, a low one for the Earth, quiet when the ground hides them.
And a short game for students: the launch slips, you pick a site, and the app shows the real answer.
What it can't tell you: the eighty-metre terrain is coarse and can be too hopeful. The needs are examples, and fragile answers can flip.
Slipday. Know your margin before the date moves.
